1.modern-en: Antigone summons her sister Ismene outside the palace gates and reveals Creon's edict forbidding the burial of their brother Polyneices. When Ismene refuses to help, Antigone declares she will bury him alone, whatever the cost.

5.modern-en: Caught in the act of pouring burial rites over Polyneices' body, Antigone is brought before Creon and admits her guilt without flinching. She argues that divine law outranks mortal decree, and refuses to show remorse even as Creon condemns her to death.

9.modern-en: Led away to be entombed alive, Antigone laments that she will die unwed and unmourned, yet insists she acted rightly in honoring her brother. She exits to her living tomb, speaking her final words of grief and defiance.

1.modern-en: Ismene refuses to join Antigone's plan, urging that they are powerless women who must obey the king or face destruction. She parts from her sister in fear, though she clearly loves her.

5.modern-en: Summoned by Creon, Ismene tries to claim a share of Antigone's guilt so that she might die with her. Antigone sharply rejects the offer — she acted alone and will not let her sister claim credit she did not earn.

epithet.en: King of Thebes, upholder of the state

3.modern-en: Creon addresses the elders of Thebes, laying out his policy: Eteocles will be buried with honor, but Polyneices' corpse must lie unburied as punishment for treason. When a guard reports that someone has already sprinkled dust over the body, Creon explodes in fury and threatens death.

5.modern-en: Creon confronts Antigone after she is caught, and they argue over whether divine law supersedes royal decree. He condemns her to death and summons Ismene, unmoved by either sister's pleas.

7.modern-en: Creon clashes bitterly with his son Haemon, who urges him to heed the people's sympathy for Antigone. Creon refuses to back down, insisting that surrendering to a woman would destroy his authority.

8.modern-en: Creon declares his final judgment: Antigone alone will die, entombed alive in a cave with just enough food to avoid blood-guilt for the state.

9.modern-en: The prophet Teiresias arrives and warns Creon that the gods are enraged by his refusal to bury Polyneices. Creon dismisses the warning as corrupt self-interest and defiantly holds his course.

10.modern-en: Shaken at last by Teiresias's prophecy, Creon is persuaded by the Chorus to relent. He rushes off to free Antigone and bury Polyneices, but he has waited too long.

11.modern-en: Creon returns from the tomb having lost everything: Antigone has hanged herself, Haemon has fallen on his own sword, and Eurydice has stabbed herself cursing his name. He is left utterly broken, begging for death.

7.modern-en: Haemon comes before his father outwardly deferential but steadily argues that Antigone is admired by the people, that wise rulers listen, and that Creon is making a fatal mistake. When Creon refuses to yield and threatens to kill Antigone in front of him, Haemon storms out vowing they will never meet again.

11.modern-en: A messenger reports that Haemon was found in the tomb beside the dead Antigone. He lunged at his father with his sword, missed, then turned the blade on himself and died with her in his arms.

Eurydice emerges from the palace having overheard the messenger's account of Haemon's death. She listens in silence and then withdraws without a word. A second messenger reveals she has stabbed herself at the altar, cursing Creon as the killer of her children.

9.modern-en: The blind seer Teiresias, guided by a boy, arrives to warn Creon that the gods have turned against him: the birds and sacrificial fires give no good omens because Polyneices' corpse lies rotting unburied. He urges Creon to relent, and when Creon accuses him of taking bribes, Teiresias prophesies that Creon will pay for his sins with the life of his own child.
